turns.question: What does INVEST stand for?
turns.text:
INVEST is Bill Wake's acronym for six attributes of a good user story: **Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimatable, Small, Testable** [S1][S3].

- **Independent:** stories can be built in any order, so they can be prioritised and estimated separately [S3].
- **Negotiable:** the card is a reminder, not a specification; detail is agreed in conversation [S3].
- **Valuable:** someone who uses or pays for the software can see why they want it [S2][S3].
- **Estimatable:** developers can make a reasonable guess at size [S2].
- **Small:** the story fits comfortably in an iteration, without being so tiny that writing it down costs more than doing it [S2].
- **Testable:** there is a way to show the story is finished [S2].

turns.question: Do partially finished stories count toward velocity?
turns.text:
No. Partly finished stories count for zero toward velocity. The *User Stories Applied* study notes say that only stories that pass their acceptance tests count, and that "partly finished stories count for nothing" [S2]. The reasons given are that estimating a percentage complete is unreliable, incomplete work has no value to users, and the last part of a story can hide a lot of difficulty [S1].

The same notes add some practical guidance:
- If partial stories regularly affect velocity, the stories are probably too big [S1].
- If many stories end an iteration half-done, it is better to finish some and leave others unstarted [S1].
- Use the points assigned during planning. Don't rescore a story because it turned out harder; apply that learning to future estimates [S1].

The Scrum Guide (2020) makes a related point about the Definition of Done. Work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done, and a backlog item that doesn't meet it cannot be released or presented at the Sprint Review [S12]. The passages I found don't mention velocity directly, so that part of the answer rests on the study notes.

Increment An Increment is a concrete stepping stone toward the Product Goal. Each Increment is additive to all prior Increments and thoroughly verified, ensuring that all Increments work together. In order to provide value, the Increment must be usable.

The Definition of Done creates transparency by providing everyone a shared understanding of what work was completed as part of the Increment. If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review.

turns.question: How do I set up user stories in Jira?
turns.text:
The documents I have don't cover how to configure Jira. They don't include steps for issue types, fields, boards, or backlog setup in any tool.

They do cover how to write and organise stories, which you can apply in Jira:

- **Story format:** The Connextra template has three slots: the role, what they want, and the business reason. [S11]
- **Structure:** A story has a card (one or two sentences for planning), conversation (the discussion that fills in details), and confirmation (acceptance tests). [S8]
- **Size and scope:** Write closed stories that end with the user achieving something definite. Avoid "manage," since managing never finishes. Keep small, specific stories for the next few iterations and broader ones for later. [S11]
- **Splitting:** Split compound stories by operation or data, and slice so each piece runs through every layer and delivers something usable. [S4, S11]
- **Bugs:** Treat a bug report as a story. Schedule large fixes like any other story, and bundle small ones under a cover card. [S6]
- **Backlog:** In Scrum, the product backlog is the prioritised list of everything wanted, and the sprint backlog is the task list for the current sprint. [S9]
- **Tools:** The Agile Methods notes mention that an Agile Office can manage tools such as Jira, Trello and Monday.com, but they don't explain how to set them up. [S7]

For Jira-specific setup, such as creating a story issue type, adding acceptance-criteria fields, or configuring a backlog board, check Atlassian's own documentation. That isn't from the library.

sources.excerpt: Chapter 3. User Role Modeling In brief: identify the distinct kinds of user before writing stories, so the product is not built for a single imagined user. Teams often write every story from one viewpoint and so miss the needs of anyone who does not fit it. Borrowing from usage-centred design (Constantine and Lockwood) and interaction design (Cooper), the chapter recommends a short role-modeling session. A user role is a set of characteristics shared by a group of users and the way they will interact with the system. The four steps Brainstorm. Customer and developers write role names on cards and place them on a table or wall, saying only the name. No discussion or judging. About fifteen minutes is usually enough. Organise. Move the cards so that overlapping roles physically overlap, by as much as the roles do. Consolidate. Discuss overlapping cards; merge or tear up duplicates. Also discard roles that will not affect the product's success. Refine. Add distinguishing attributes to each remaining card.

Asking how fast a feature must be implies that there is a speed requirement; asking what performance matters, and where, does not. Start broad and move to specific questions later. Take one role or persona at a time. Starting from an empty box for the main screen, ask what that user can do from there; each answer becomes a new box and a story.

turns.question: Does the Daily Scrum still use the three questions?
turns.text:
No. The 2020 Scrum Guide doesn't prescribe any fixed questions. It says the Developers "can select whatever structure and techniques they want," as long as the Daily Scrum focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day of work [S4]. The purpose is to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the Sprint Backlog [S4].

The three-question format appears in the other sources:

- **User Stories Applied study notes** describe the daily scrum as a meeting where each person says what they did yesterday, what they will do today, and what is in their way [S1]. That summary describes older practice, so it's not the current Scrum rule.
- **Agile Methods study notes** present the three daily questions as standard [S5], but the same notes acknowledge that the 2020 Scrum Guide leaves the format to the Developers [S5].

So the three questions are a common format, not a current Scrum requirement.

turns.text:
A persona is an invented, named individual who represents an important user role [S1]. A user role is a group of users with shared characteristics and a shared way of using the system [S2].

- **In design thinking:** Personas are fictional users based on real data, and they are one of the tools used in the Empathise and Define phases [S3].
- **Caveat:** The User Stories Applied notes say personas are optional. For a small project they are probably not worth the effort [S5].

turns.question: Qu'est-ce qu'une user story ?
turns.text:
Une user story est une courte description d'une fonctionnalité qui compte pour une personne qui utilise ou achète le système. Elle est décrite comme ayant trois aspects : la carte, la conversation et la confirmation [S5].

- **Carte** : une ou deux phrases, traditionnellement écrites sur une fiche, qui servent à la planification et de rappel [S5].
- **Conversation** : les échanges entre le client et les développeurs où les détails se précisent [S5].
- **Confirmation** : les tests qui capturent ces détails et montrent quand la story est terminée [S7].

Le gabarit le plus répandu, issu de l'équipe XP de Connextra, comporte trois éléments : le rôle, ce que la personne veut, et la raison métier [S10]. Il s'écrit donc en général « En tant que [rôle], je veux [action] afin de [bénéfice] ».

Quelques points clés :

- **Une story doit avoir de la valeur pour un utilisateur ou un acheteur.** Une décision technique qui n'intéresse pas les utilisateurs n'en est pas une pour une application métier ordinaire [S7].
- **La carte n'est pas une spécification.** Elle sert de rappel pour parler ; les tests consignent ce qui a été décidé. Les stories ne sont pas des contrats [S16][S7].
- **Les stories se vérifient avec INVEST** : indépendante, négociable, valorisable, estimable, petite et testable [S8].
- **Les très grandes stories sont des epics** et doivent être découpées avant d'être réalisées. Une story devrait représenter entre une demi-journée et environ deux semaines de travail pour un développeur ou une paire [S7].

turns.question: When should a team use Kanban instead of Scrum?
turns.text:
Use Kanban when work arrives continuously and unpredictably, and Scrum when work can be planned in fixed cycles.

- **Kanban fits** continuous, unpredictable flows of small items, such as support and maintenance, and products that face continual change and many inputs [S6][S4][S3]. The guide's example is a help desk, "because its work arrives continuously and unpredictably" [S5]. Kanban has no timeboxed cycles, and the plan can change at any time [S6].
- **Scrum fits** long-term, complex projects where feedback may change requirements, the amount of work can't be estimated exactly, and the release date isn't fixed [S6]. It also suits a close-knit team that delivers in iterations [S3].
- **Kanban is less suited** to teams that need the structure of fixed goals and roles [S14].
- **A middle option:** Scrumban combines Scrum's structure with Kanban's flexibility, for teams that deliver often but need looser cycles [S3].

The study notes also say to pick the method that fits the people, goals and environment rather than the best-known name, and then keep adjusting it [S5]. The Scrum Guide itself doesn't cover Kanban [S9], so the Kanban guidance above comes from the Agile Methods study notes, which draw on secondary overviews.

turns.question: What are the three Kanban metrics?
turns.text:
The three Kanban metrics are:

- **Cycle time:** the time from when work on a task starts to when it is completed [S1].
- **Lead time:** the time from when a task is requested to when it is delivered, including time spent waiting to be started [S1].
- **Throughput:** the number of tasks completed in a given period [S1].

Cap how many tasks may be under way at once, so the team finishes before starting. This shortens cycle time. Manage flow. Aim for tasks to complete quickly without overload, and measure flow. Improve continuously. Use flow data to find bottlenecks, then adjust WIP limits, the board, or working practices. Lead time Time from when a task is requested to when it is delivered, including time spent waiting to be started. Throughput Number of tasks completed in a given period. Kanban defines no specific roles. The guide suggests a Service Delivery Manager to oversee the process and improve flow, and possibly a Product Owner to prioritise the backlog. C5. Lean comes from the Toyota Production System.

Seeing everyone's contribution helps the team focus on finishing work well and on time. Some organisations (8%) combine Scrum and Kanban as Scrumban. B7. Hybrid In brief: use waterfall where planning matters and agile where flexibility matters. Agile is iterative and flexible; waterfall is step by step, needs careful planning and resists change. Some organisations find that combining them works better than choosing one. A common split: waterfall for budgeting, planning and hardware set-up; agile for software development and testing.

sources.excerpt: Cooperation with the client The customer is closely involved and can change requirements or accept the team's suggestions. Benefits reported in the survey the paper cites: ability to manage changing priorities (88% of respondents), higher team productivity (83%) and better project visibility (83%). Takeaway Agile is an umbrella term. What the frameworks share is short cycles, close teamwork, customer involvement and a willingness to change scope. B4. Six frameworks side by side In brief: the paper's own summary table, condensed, with its adoption figures and its advice on when each framework fits. Framework Key features When to use Share of organisations using it Scrum Work is cut into sprints of one to four weeks. The team follows a plan for each sprint. People have predefined roles. Long-term, complex projects where stakeholder feedback may change requirements, the amount of work cannot be estimated exactly, and the release date is not fixed. 58% exclusively; a further 18% combined with other techniques Kanban Built on visualising the workflow. Work in progress is prioritised and limited. No timeboxed cycles. The plan can change at any time.

sources.title: Agile Methods: Study Notes
sources.excerpt: The modes need different skills, techniques and tools, so two separate groups are used. They report through different structures but must communicate. Each depends on the other: Mode 2 uses the information and services that Mode 1 provides, and Mode 1 relies on Mode 2 to test new product ideas and development methods. B9. Lean In brief: deliver more value with less effort, investment and time by removing whatever does not add value. Lean shares its origins with Kanban in the Toyota Production System. Mary and Tom Poppendieck applied it to software in their book Lean Software Development, with seven principles: Principle Meaning Eliminate waste Waste is anything that adds no value to the project. In software that includes idle time, unneeded features and defects. Amplify learning and create knowledge Development is a continuous learning process. Developers rarely get code right first time and learn by solving problems and producing variations. Decide as late as possible Later decisions rest on more facts. With technology dating quickly, it is wise to delay irreversible design choices and keep capacity for change.
